tagline: A governor’s namesake road follows the railroad toward the Alaska Range
intro: The Parks Highway mostly parallels the Alaska Railroad, crossing the Alaska Range through Broad Pass. Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights mountain views, Denali State Park, Hurricane Gulch and access to Denali National Park and Preserve. At Broad Pass, the state transportation department puts the crossing at 2,400 feet. The highway is signed as Alaska Route 3.

Completed in 1971 as the Anchorage-Fairbanks Highway, the road received its current name in 1975. It honors George Alexander Parks, Alaska’s territorial governor from 1925 to 1933. For Nenana, completion meant a shorter, direct route to Anchorage, following a 1968 road bridge that had replaced the Tanana River ferry. The highway’s mileposts preserve a connection to the older approach from Anchorage: they begin at Mile 35 where the Parks and Glenn highways meet near Palmer. The numbers measure distance from downtown Anchorage, although the Parks Highway itself never enters the city.

Traveling north through Denali State Park, Byers Lake and the adjacent Alaska Veterans Memorial precede Hurricane Gulch and Broad Pass. Cantwell stands at the pass’s northern boundary. Farther north, the highway reaches the Nenana River valley at Denali Park, with the national park’s visitor center west along the park road. Healy comes next, and the highway continues through Nenana toward Fairbanks.

moments.title: Byers Lake
moments.text: Before highway access, bush pilot Don Sheldon repeatedly flew a fisherman to this lake in the 1950s; the lake bears that fisherman’s name. Byers Lake is now accessible from the Parks Highway inside Denali State Park. The small lake lies 28 miles north of Talkeetna in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough. A developed campground, public-use cabins and a small boat dock serve the lakeshore. On the adjacent hilltop stands the Alaska Veterans Memorial, another stop highlighted by the state’s scenic-byways program. In summer, the lake is home to trumpeter swans and common loons.

moments.title: Hurricane Gulch
moments.text: Two bridges share the Hurricane Gulch name: the road bridge is upstream and slightly east of the railroad bridge. The railroad’s steel arch stretches 918 feet across the gulch, 296 feet above Hurricane Creek. American Bridge Company crews began work in early 1921, stringing an aerial tram across the gap so construction could proceed from both sides. The first passenger train crossed on August 15 that year. Passenger trains and freight movements use the railroad crossing. For road travelers, Alaska DOT identifies a viewpoint at the south end of the highway bridge.

moments.title: Broad Pass
moments.text: Broad Pass is an approximately 15-mile gap through the Alaska Range, with Cantwell at its northern boundary. The gap separates the Alaska Range to the west from an unnamed subrange to the east. The Dena knew the area for millennia. USGS geologists George Homans Eldridge and Robert Muldrow recorded its geology and topography during an expedition in 1898; railway plans followed in 1902. The Anchorage-Fairbanks railroad was completed in 1923, followed by highway access in 1971. Alaska DOT highlights the pass for views of the Alaska Range.
